hello.title: Hello, Go!
hello.summary: Write your first Go program and print text and numbers with fmt.Println and fmt.Printf.
hello.lesson.0: Every Go program is made of **packages**. A program that you can run uses `package main` and has a function called `main`. Go starts the program there.
hello.lesson.2: Line by line: `package main` says that this file belongs to the main package. `import "fmt"` loads the `fmt` package, which can print text. `func main()` defines the function where the program starts. Its code goes between the braces `{` and `}`.
hello.lesson.4: `fmt.Println` prints its values, puts a space between them and ends the line. Text goes in double quotes, numbers do not. `fmt.Println()` without values prints an empty line.
hello.lesson.6: Go can calculate for you. `2 + 3` without quotes is a calculation, but `"2 + 3"` in quotes is only text. Use `*` to multiply and `/` to divide.
hello.lesson.9: `fmt.Printf` prints a **format string** and fills in values. Each verb is a placeholder: `%s` for text, `%d` for a whole number and `%v` for any value. `Printf` does not end the line, so you add `\n` (a new line) yourself.
hello.lesson.11: Go is strict about tidy code. If you import a package and do not use it, the program does not compile. A line that starts with `//` is a comment, and Go ignores it.
hello.lesson.12: The opening brace `{` must be on the same line as `func main()`. Go ends lines with an invisible semicolon, so a brace on the next line is an error. Go is also case sensitive: `Println` works, `println` from `fmt` does not.
hello.card.0: `package main` + `func main()` make a runnable program
hello.card.2: `fmt.Println(a, b)` prints with spaces and a new line
hello.card.3: `fmt.Printf("%s %d %v\n", s, n, x)` fills in values
hello-1.prompt: Which function does Go run when the program starts?
hello-1.explain: A runnable program starts in the function `main` of the package `main`.
hello-2.explain: `Println` puts a space between its values.
hello-3.explain: `10-4` has no quotes, so Go calculates `6`. Then `Println` adds a space and the text.
hello-4.explain: `Printf` prints exactly the format string. You need `\n` at the end to start a new line.
hello-5.prompt: Complete the program so it compiles and prints Hi.
hello-5.explain: The package name goes in double quotes: `import "fmt"`.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Name: Ada`.
hello-6.explain: `%s` is the placeholder for a string. `%d` only works for whole numbers.
hello-7.prompt: Build the line that prints Hello, Go! on its own line.
hello-7.explain: The function is `fmt.Println` with a capital P. The text goes in double quotes inside the parentheses.

hello-8.explain: First the package, then the imports, then the function `main` with its code between the braces.

hello-10.explain: The closing quote is missing. Write `fmt.Println("Stop")`.

hello-12.explain: Each `%d` is replaced by the next value. `2+3` is calculated first, so the last value is `5`.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in variables, get to know int, float64, string and bool, and convert between types.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** stores a value under a name. With `var` you write the name, the type and the value: `var age int = 13`.
variables.lesson.2: Inside a function you usually write the short form `:=`. Go finds the type from the value. To change a variable later, use `=`. `count++` adds 1, `count--` subtracts 1, and `count += 10` adds 10 (there are also `-=` and `*=`).
variables.lesson.4: `:=` creates a **new** variable, so you can use it only once per name. Go also refuses to compile a program with a variable that is declared but never used.
variables.lesson.6: The most common types are `int` (whole numbers), `float64` (decimal numbers), `string` (text) and `bool` (`true` or `false`). The verb `%T` in `Printf` prints the type of a value.
variables.lesson.8: A variable without a value gets the **zero value** of its type: `0` for numbers, `""` (the empty string) for `string` and `false` for `bool`. The verb `%q` prints a string in quotes, so you can see the empty string.
variables.lesson.10: A **constant** is declared with `const`. Its value is fixed and can never change. The operator `+` adds numbers and also joins strings.
variables.lesson.12: Go never mixes types by itself. To convert, write the type like a function: `float64(n)` or `int(x)`. Dividing two `int` values gives an `int`, so `7 / 2` is `3`. `int(1.99)` cuts off the decimals and gives `1`.
variables.card.0: `x := 5` declares a variable and sets it
variables.card.1: `var s string` gets the zero value `""`
variables-1.explain: Both values are `int`, so the division drops the rest: 10 / 4 is 2.
variables-2.explain: `count` starts with the zero value `0`. Then 5 is added.
variables-3.prompt: What is the zero value of a `bool`?
variables-3.explain: Every type has a zero value. For `bool` it is `false`.
variables-4.explain: A number with a decimal point gets the type `float64` when you use `:=`.
variables-5.explain: `limit` is a constant. You cannot assign a new value to a constant.
variables-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 3.5.
variables-6.explain: `float64(a)` converts 7 to a decimal number, so the division keeps the .5. With `int` you get 3.
variables-7.prompt: Complete the code so `rate` can never change.

variables-8.prompt: Use `var` to declare `price` of type `float64` with the value `4.5`.

variables-9.explain: 3 times 4 is 12, plus 3 is 15. In the other order you get (3 + 3) * 4 = 24.

variables-12.explain: `count` is an `int` and `price` is a `float64`. Go does not mix them: write `float64(count) * price`.
control.title: Control flow
control.summary: Make decisions with if and switch, and repeat code with the different forms of the for loop.
control.lesson.0: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. Go needs no parentheses around the condition, but the braces are required. You compare with `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`, and combine conditions with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not).
control.lesson.2: An `if` can start with a short statement, followed by a semicolon. A variable created there exists only inside the `if` and its `else` branches. The operator `%` gives the rest of a division, so `n%2 == 0` checks for an even number.
control.lesson.5: Go has only one loop keyword: `for`. The classic form has three parts: a start statement, a condition and a statement that runs after each round.
control.lesson.7: With only a condition, `for` repeats while the condition is `true`. Other languages call this a while loop. `for { }` without a condition repeats forever, until a `break`.
control.lesson.9: `for i := range 6` counts from `0` to `5`. `continue` jumps to the next round, and `break` ends the loop at once.
control.lesson.12: `switch` compares a value with several cases and runs the first one that matches. A case can list several values. Go stops after the matching case, so you need no `break`. `default` runs when no case matches. A `switch` without a value checks conditions, like a chain of `if` and `else if`.
control.card.1: `if v := f(); v > 0 { }` runs a statement first
control-1.explain: 8 is not greater than 10, but it is greater than 5, so the `else if` branch runs.
control-3.prompt: How many lines does this print?
control-3.explain: `i` takes the values 10, 7, 4 and 1. The next value, -2, is not greater than 0.
control-4.explain: Only the matching case runs. Go does not continue into the next case.
control-5.explain: `n` is created in the `if` statement, so it exists only inside the `if`. The last line cannot use it.

control-7.explain: 7 % 2 is 1, so `n%2 == 0` is `false` and the `else` branch prints `odd`. A single `=` is an assignment, not a comparison.

control-8.explain: Go has no `while`. A `for` with only a condition does the same job.

control-9.explain: The loop counts from 0 to 4, and the `if` inside the loop prints only the even numbers.

control-12.explain: A comparison needs two equals signs: `if x == 4 {`. A single `=` assigns a value.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions with parameters, return one or more values, and accept any number of arguments.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** gives a piece of code a name. You define it with `func`, outside of `main`, and call it by its name. Each parameter has a name followed by its type.
functions.lesson.2: The result type comes after the parentheses. `return` sends a value back to the caller. When parameters share a type, you write it once: `a, b int`.
functions.lesson.4: Arguments must match the parameter types exactly. `add(2.5, 1)` does not compile, because `add` expects `int` values.
functions.lesson.6: A Go function can return several values. List their types in parentheses. The caller receives them with `q, r := divide(17, 5)`. The blank name `_` throws away a value you do not need.
functions.lesson.8: The order of functions in a file does not matter. You can define `divide` below `main` and still call it from `main`.
functions.lesson.10: A **variadic** function accepts any number of values. Write `...` before the type of the last parameter. Inside the function, `nums` holds all the values, and `for _, n := range nums` visits each one. You learn more about this in the next world.
functions.lesson.12: You already know a variadic function: `fmt.Println` accepts any number of values. That is why `fmt.Println(1, "a", true)` works.
functions.card.0: `func add(a, b int) int { return a + b }`
functions.card.3: `func sum(nums ...int)` takes any number of ints
functions-2.explain: 9 is not less than 4, so the function returns `b, a`, which is 4 and 9.
functions-3.prompt: Which line correctly starts a function that takes two `int` values and returns an `int`?
functions-3.explain: In Go the type comes after the parameter name, and the result type comes after the parentheses.
functions-4.explain: `_` throws away the first result, so `year` gets the second one.
functions-5.explain: The function promises an `int` result but has no `return`. Go reports a missing return.
functions-6.prompt: Complete the function so it returns two values.
functions-6.explain: Several result types go in parentheses: `(int, int)`.
functions-7.prompt: Complete the function so it accepts any number of names.
functions-7.explain: A variadic parameter has three dots before its type: `names ...string`.

functions-8.explain: `:=` declares both new variables, and each one gets one of the two results.

slices.title: Slices and maps
slices.summary: Keep many values in arrays, slices and maps: add, read, loop over and delete elements.
slices.lesson.0: An **array** has a fixed length that is part of its type: `[3]int` holds exactly three `int` values. A **slice** like `[]string` has no fixed length and can grow. You read an element by its index, and the first index is `0`. `len` gives the number of elements.
slices.lesson.2: `append` adds values to a slice and returns the new slice, so you assign the result back. `s[1:3]` takes the elements from index `1` up to, but not including, index `3`.
slices.lesson.4: An index that does not exist stops the program with a **panic** (a run-time error). With three elements, `names[3]` panics, because the last index is `2`.
slices.lesson.6: `for i, v := range s` visits every element: `i` is the index and `v` the value. Write `_` instead of `i` when you do not need the index.
slices.lesson.9: A **map** stores pairs of keys and values. `map[string]int` has `string` keys and `int` values. `m[key] = value` adds a pair or changes it, `delete(m, key)` removes it, and `len(m)` counts the pairs.
slices.lesson.11: `make(map[string]int)` creates an empty map. Reading a missing key gives the zero value. To find out if a key exists, read two values: `v, ok := m[key]`. `ok` is `true` only when the key is in the map.
slices.lesson.13: `for k, v := range m` loops over a map, but the order changes from run to run. `fmt.Println` prints maps with sorted keys. A map declared with `var m map[string]int` is `nil`, and writing to it panics, so create maps with `make` or `{}`.
slices.card.4: `v, ok := m[key]` checks if a key exists
slices-1.explain: After `append` the slice has 4 elements, and the new value 16 has index 3.
slices-2.explain: `[1:4]` starts at index 1 (`b`) and stops before index 4 (`e`).
slices-3.explain: `x` is now 5 and `y` is 2. The missing key `z` gives the zero value 0, so the sum is 7.
slices-4.statement: `append(s, 5)` changes `s` directly, so you do not need to use its result.
slices-4.explain: `append` returns the new slice. You must assign it: `s = append(s, 5)`. Go does not even compile a call whose result is not used.
slices-5.explain: The key `b` is not in the map, so `ok` is `false`. The map has one pair.
slices-6.prompt: Complete the code so it removes `Ana` from the map and prints 0.
slices-6.explain: The built-in function `delete(m, key)` removes a key from a map.
slices-7.prompt: Complete the loop so it adds up the values (the result is 15).
slices-7.explain: `range` gives the index first and the value second. `_, n` skips the index and keeps the value.
slices-8.prompt: Build the line that adds `"kiwi"` to the slice `fruits`.
slices-8.explain: `append` returns the longer slice, and you assign it back to `fruits` with `=`.

structs.title: Structs and methods
structs.summary: Group data in your own struct types and add methods with value and pointer receivers.
structs.lesson.0: A **struct** groups several values, called **fields**, into one new type. You define it with `type Name struct { ... }`, create a value with `Book{Title: "Go Basics", Pages: 120}` and reach a field with a dot: `b.Title`. The verb `%+v` prints a struct with its field names.
structs.lesson.2: Fields that you do not set get their zero value. Fields of the same type can share one line: `X, Y int`.
structs.lesson.5: A **method** is a function that belongs to a type. It has a **receiver** in parentheses before its name: `func (r Rect) Area() float64`. You call it with a dot: `r.Area()`.
structs.lesson.8: A **value receiver** like `(c Counter)` gets a copy, so its changes are lost. A **pointer receiver** like `(c *Counter)` works on the original value and can change it. When you call `c.Inc()` on a variable, Go passes the pointer for you.
structs.lesson.10: `&` gives the address of a value, which is a **pointer**. `&Player{Name: "Ana"}` has the type `*Player`. You use the same dot to reach fields and methods through a pointer.
structs.lesson.12: A good rule: use a pointer receiver when the method changes the struct. If one method of a type needs a pointer receiver, give all its methods pointer receivers.
structs.card.2: `func (r Rect) Area() float64`: value receiver (a copy)
structs-1.explain: `d.Age++` adds 1 to the field `Age`, so 3 becomes 4.
structs-2.explain: `H` is not set, so it has the zero value 0. `Println` prints the fields in braces.
structs-3.explain: `Switch` has a value receiver, so it changes a copy. The original `l.On` stays `false`.
structs-4.prompt: Which method can change the fields of the original `Account`?
structs-4.explain: Only a pointer receiver works on the original value. The other forms get a copy.
structs-5.statement: `fmt.Printf("%+v\n", p)` prints the struct `p` together with its field names.
structs-5.explain: `%v` prints only the values, `%+v` adds the field names, for example `{X:1 Y:2}`.
structs-6.prompt: Complete the receiver so the program prints 10.
structs-6.explain: With the pointer receiver `*Wallet`, `Add` changes the original wallet. With `Wallet` it would change a copy and print 0.
structs-7.prompt: Complete the line so it creates a `City`.

interfaces.title: Interfaces
interfaces.summary: Describe behavior with interfaces, make your types printable with fmt.Stringer and check types with a type switch.
interfaces.lesson.0: An **interface** is a list of methods. Every type that has these methods satisfies the interface automatically. There is no `implements` keyword. A slice of an interface type can hold values of different types.
interfaces.lesson.2: A function with an interface parameter accepts every type that satisfies the interface. The function only uses the methods of the interface.
interfaces.lesson.4: A method with a pointer receiver belongs to the pointer type only. If `Speak` had the receiver `*Dog`, then `&Dog{}` would satisfy `Speaker`, but `Dog{}` would not.
interfaces.lesson.6: The `fmt` package defines the interface `fmt.Stringer` with one method: `String() string`. When your type has this method, `fmt.Println` and `%v` use it. `fmt.Sprintf` works like `Printf`, but it returns the text instead of printing it.
interfaces.lesson.9: The type `any` has no methods, so it can hold a value of any type. A **type switch** `switch v := x.(type)` checks which type the value really has. Inside each case, `v` has the type of that case.
interfaces.lesson.11: To check for one single type, use a **type assertion** with two results: `s, ok := x.(string)`. If `x` holds a `string`, `ok` is `true`. Otherwise `ok` is `false` and `s` gets the zero value.
interfaces.lesson.13: Keep interfaces small. Many useful interfaces in Go have only one method, like `fmt.Stringer`.
interfaces.card.1: A type satisfies an interface by having its methods (no `implements`)
interfaces.card.4: `s, ok := x.(string)` is a type assertion
interfaces-1.explain: `Cat` has the method `Sound() string`, so it satisfies `Animal`. The call runs the method of `Cat`.
interfaces-2.explain: `Point` has a `String` method, so `fmt.Println` uses it instead of printing `{2 5}`.
interfaces-3.explain: `3.5` is a `float64`, not an `int` or a `string`, so the `default` case runs.

interfaces-4.options.3: It is defined in the same file as the interface

errors.title: Errors
errors.summary: Handle errors the Go way: check if err != nil, create errors with errors.New and fmt.Errorf, and return them.
errors.lesson.0: In Go an error is a normal value of the type `error`. A function that can fail returns an `error` as its **last** result. The value `nil` means that there was no error. `strconv.Atoi` converts text to an `int` and returns such an error.
errors.lesson.2: Check the error right after the call with `if err != nil`. Handle the problem there, for example with `continue` or `return`. The normal code continues after the `if`.
errors.lesson.4: When `err` is not `nil`, the other results usually hold zero values. Do not use them before you have checked the error.
errors.lesson.6: `errors.New` creates an error with a fixed message. Your function returns it as the last value, and returns `nil` when everything works. Error messages start with a lowercase letter and have no period at the end.
errors.lesson.8: `fmt.Errorf` builds the message with verbs, like `fmt.Sprintf`, and returns an `error`.
errors.lesson.11: Often a function cannot fix an error itself. It returns the error to its caller and adds context with the verb `%w`, which wraps the original error. `errors.Is(err, target)` checks if `err` is `target` or wraps it.
errors.lesson.13: Handle each error once: either print it, or return it to the caller. Doing both prints the same problem twice.
errors.card.0: `func f() (int, error)`: the error is the last result
errors-1.explain: "12" is a valid number, so `n` is 12 and `err` is `nil`, which prints as `<nil>`.
errors-2.explain: `check(5)` returns `nil`. `check(50)` returns an error with the message `50 is too big`.

errors-5.explain: By convention the `error` is the **last** result, for example `(int, error)`.

errors-12.explain: The error branch must run when there is an error: `if err != nil {`.
